claim: SMC complexes are widely conserved ATP-powered DNA-loop-extrusion motors indispensable for organizing and faithfully segregating chromosomes.
source: SMC complexes are widely conserved ATP-powered DNA-loop-extrusion motors indispensable for organizing and faithfully segregating chromosomes.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus about SMC complexes.

claim: The number, strength, and distribution of Smc loading sites influence bacterial chromosome organization by modulating the probability of Smc collisions.
source: These factors include the number, the strength, and the distribution of Smc loading sites, the residency time on the chromosome, the translocation rate, and the cellular abundance of Smc complexes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript showing effects of parS site manipulation.

claim: The residency time on the chromosome influences bacterial chromosome organization by modulating the probability of Smc collisions.
source: These factors include the number, the strength, and the distribution of Smc loading sites, the residency time on the chromosome, the translocation rate, and the cellular abundance of Smc complexes.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental observations with modified Smc proteins and their chromosomal distribution patterns.

claim: The translocation rate influences bacterial chromosome organization by modulating the probability of Smc collisions.
source: These factors include the number, the strength, and the distribution of Smc loading sites, the residency time on the chromosome, the translocation rate, and the cellular abundance of Smc complexes.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq time-course experiments showing different translocation dynamics.

claim: The cellular abundance of Smc complexes influences bacterial chromosome organization by modulating the probability of Smc collisions.
source: These factors include the number, the strength, and the distribution of Smc loading sites, the residency time on the chromosome, the translocation rate, and the cellular abundance of Smc complexes.
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by experiments with SMChigh strains showing altered chromosome organization.

claim: These parameters are fine-tuned to reduce the frequency of encounters between Smc complexes as a risk mitigation strategy.
source: By studying various mutants, we show that these parameters are fine-tuned to reduce the frequency of encounters between Smc complexes, presumably as a risk mitigation strategy.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that perturbations lead to defects, suggesting optimization under normal conditions.

claim: Mild perturbations hamper chromosome organization by causing Smc collisions.
source: Mild perturbations hamper chromosome organization by causing Smc collisions, implying that the cellular capacity to resolve them is limited.
evidence: This is supported by 3C-seq data showing disrupted chromosome arm alignment in various mutants.

claim: The cellular capacity to resolve Smc collisions is limited.
source: Mild perturbations hamper chromosome organization by causing Smc collisions, implying that the cellular capacity to resolve them is limited.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that increased collision frequency leads to organizational defects.

claim: Loop extrusion can explain formation of topologically associated domains (TADs) in interphase.
source: Loop extrusion can explain diverse folding phenomena across all domains of life: formation of topologically associated domains (TADs) in interphase, lengthwise compacted chromosomes during mitosis, as well as juxtaposition of the arms of bacterial chromosomes.
evidence: This is based on established scientific understanding of SMC complex function.

claim: Loop extrusion can explain lengthwise compacted chromosomes during mitosis.
source: Loop extrusion can explain diverse folding phenomena across all domains of life: formation of topologically associated domains (TADs) in interphase, lengthwise compacted chromosomes during mitosis, as well as juxtaposition of the arms of bacterial chromosomes.
evidence: This is based on established scientific understanding of SMC complex function.

claim: Loop extrusion can explain juxtaposition of the arms of bacterial chromosomes.
source: Loop extrusion can explain diverse folding phenomena across all domains of life: formation of topologically associated domains (TADs) in interphase, lengthwise compacted chromosomes during mitosis, as well as juxtaposition of the arms of bacterial chromosomes.
evidence: This is based on established scientific understanding and is directly relevant to the study organism.

claim: Purified yeast condensin extrudes DNA loops at rates of ~1 kb/s in an asymmetric (one-sided) manner.
source: Purified yeast condensin and vertebrate cohesin extrude DNA loops at rates of ~1 kb/s in an asymmetric (one-sided) or symmetric (two-sided) manner, respectively (Davidson et al., 2019; Ganji et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by cited single-molecule experiments.

claim: Vertebrate cohesin extrudes DNA loops at rates of ~1 kb/s in a symmetric (two-sided) manner.
source: Purified yeast condensin and vertebrate cohesin extrude DNA loops at rates of ~1 kb/s in an asymmetric (one-sided) or symmetric (two-sided) manner, respectively (Davidson et al., 2019; Ganji et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by cited single-molecule experiments.

claim: Two DNA-loop-extruding yeast condensin complexes on the same DNA molecule occasionally traverse one another in vitro, forming interlocking loops (Z loops).
source: In the case of yeast condensin, two DNA-loop-extruding complexes on the same DNA molecule were reported to occasionally traverse one another in vitro, thus forming interlocking loops (also termed Z loops) (Kim et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on a cited in vitro study.

claim: Z-loop formation could improve the otherwise poor loop coverage achieved by one-sided motors.
source: In principle, the latter behavior could improve the otherwise poor loop coverage achieved by one-sided motors, but on the other hand it likely generates undesirable DNA entanglements (such as pseudoknots) (Banigan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a theoretical consideration based on modeling studies.

claim: Z-loop formation likely generates undesirable DNA entanglements such as pseudoknots.
source: In principle, the latter behavior could improve the otherwise poor loop coverage achieved by one-sided motors, but on the other hand it likely generates undesirable DNA entanglements (such as pseudoknots) (Banigan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a theoretical consideration based on modeling studies.

claim: The biological relevance of Z-loop formation and condensin traversal is yet to be determined.
source: The biological relevance of Z-loop formation and condensin traversal is yet to be determined.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: MukBEF complexes presumably start DNA loop extrusion from randomly chosen entry sites on the bacterial chromosome.
source: One relies on MukBEF (or MksBEF) complexes, presumably starting DNA loop extrusion from randomly chosen entry sites on the bacterial chromosome (Lioy et al., 2018; Lioy et al., 2020; Mäkelä and Sherratt, 2020).
evidence: This is based on cited studies of MukBEF function.

claim: Smc-ScpAB complexes start DNA translocation from predefined entry sites, the 16 bp parS DNA sequences.
source: The second pattern occurs in most bacteria, where Smc-ScpAB complexes start DNA translocation from predefined entry sites, the 16 bp parS DNA sequences, which are generally found near the replication origin and are specifically recognized by the Smc-loader protein ParB (Gruber and Errington, 2009; Lin and Grossman, 1998; Minnen et al., 2016; Sullivan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on multiple cited studies establishing this mechanism.

claim: parS DNA sequences are generally found near the replication origin.
source: The second pattern occurs in most bacteria, where Smc-ScpAB complexes start DNA translocation from predefined entry sites, the 16 bp parS DNA sequences, which are generally found near the replication origin and are specifically recognized by the Smc-loader protein ParB (Gruber and Errington, 2009; Lin and Grossman, 1998; Minnen et al., 2016; Sullivan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on cited studies of parS distribution in bacteria.

claim: parS DNA sequences are specifically recognized by the Smc-loader protein ParB.
source: The second pattern occurs in most bacteria, where Smc-ScpAB complexes start DNA translocation from predefined entry sites, the 16 bp parS DNA sequences, which are generally found near the replication origin and are specifically recognized by the Smc-loader protein ParB (Gruber and Errington, 2009; Lin and Grossman, 1998; Minnen et al., 2016; Sullivan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on cited studies of ParB function.

claim: ParB dimers form DNA clamps that self-load onto DNA at parS sites.
source: ParB dimers form DNA clamps that self-load onto DNA at parS sites (Jalal et al., 2020; Osorio-Valeriano et al., 2019; Soh et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on recent cited studies of ParB mechanism.

claim: Smc complexes translocate away from the parS loading site in both directions (two-sided).
source: As Smc complexes translocate away from the parS loading site in both directions (two-sided), they co-align the left and the right chromosome arms that flank the replication origin (Marbouty et al., 2015; Minnen et al., 2016; Tran et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2017), eventually getting unloaded by XerD near the replication terminus (Karaboja et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on cited studies using chromosome conformation capture and other methods.

claim: Smc complexes co-align the left and right chromosome arms that flank the replication origin.
source: As Smc complexes translocate away from the parS loading site in both directions (two-sided), they co-align the left and the right chromosome arms that flank the replication origin (Marbouty et al., 2015; Minnen et al., 2016; Tran et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2017), eventually getting unloaded by XerD near the replication terminus (Karaboja et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on cited studies using chromosome conformation capture.

claim: Smc complexes get unloaded by XerD near the replication terminus.
source: As Smc complexes translocate away from the parS loading site in both directions (two-sided), they co-align the left and the right chromosome arms that flank the replication origin (Marbouty et al., 2015; Minnen et al., 2016; Tran et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2017), eventually getting unloaded by XerD near the replication terminus (Karaboja et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on a cited recent study.

claim: Bacterial genomes often have one or few closely positioned parS sites separated by a few kb.
source: Bacterial genomes often have one or few closely positioned parS sites (separated by a few kb) (Livny et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on a cited genomic survey.

claim: Bacillus subtilis harbors eight parS sites scattered over a ~0.75 Mb region of the genome.
source: Bacillus subtilis (Bsu), however, harbors eight parS sites scattered over a much wider region of the genome (~0.75 Mb) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and is an established feature of B. subtilis.

claim: Smc-CC425 supported normal growth on nutrient-rich medium even in a sensitized background (ΔparB).
source: From a collection of 20 constructs, we here identified several elongated Smc proteins, including Smc-CC425 (with a 425 aa coiled coil as compared to the 334 aa in wild-type Smc), which supported normal growth on nutrient-rich medium even in a sensitized background (ΔparB) (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by spotting assays shown in the figures.

claim: Smc-CC425 has a 425 amino acid coiled coil compared to 334 amino acids in wild-type Smc.
source: From a collection of 20 constructs, we here identified several elongated Smc proteins, including Smc-CC425 (with a 425 aa coiled coil as compared to the 334 aa in wild-type Smc), which supported normal growth on nutrient-rich medium even in a sensitized background (ΔparB) (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is a description of the engineered protein construct.

claim: Smc-HT and Smc-CC425-HT proteins show comparable cellular levels.
source: In-gel fluorescence detection showed comparable cellular levels for Smc-HT and Smc-CC425-HT proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in-gel fluorescence quantification.

claim: Chemical cross-linking of cysteine variants of Smc-CC425 indicated that it assembles holo-complexes efficiently.
source: Chemical cross-linking of cysteine variants of Smc-CC425 moreover indicated that it assembles holo-complexes efficiently, and co-isolation of cross-linked circular species with intact chromosomal DNA implied a only slightly reduced fraction of chromosomally loaded Smc-CC425 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; Vazquez Nunez et al., 2019).
evidence: This is demonstrated by chromosome co-entrapment assays.

claim: Smc-CC425 shows a slightly reduced fraction of chromosomally loaded protein compared to wild-type.
source: Chemical cross-linking of cysteine variants of Smc-CC425 moreover indicated that it assembles holo-complexes efficiently, and co-isolation of cross-linked circular species with intact chromosomal DNA implied a only slightly reduced fraction of chromosomally loaded Smc-CC425 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; Vazquez Nunez et al., 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from chromosome co-entrapment assay results.

claim: Smc-CC425 and other elongated variants failed to support normal chromosome organization.
source: We found that Smc-CC425 and the other elongated variants failed to support normal chromosome organization (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by 3C-seq contact maps.

claim: The co-alignment of chromosome arms was strongly compromised in Smc-CC425 as revealed by the absence of a secondary diagonal in 3C-seq maps.
source: As revealed by the absence of a secondary diagonal, the co-alignment of chromosome arms was strongly compromised.
evidence: This is directly observed in 3C-seq contact maps in Figure 1C.

claim: An arc of contacts on the left arm of the chromosome was observed in wild-type and mutant 3C-seq maps.
source: An arc of contacts on the left arm of the chromosome however was observed in wild-type and mutant 3C-seq maps (see below).
evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq contact maps.

claim: A control chimeric protein with wild-type arm length (Smc-CC334 Spn hinge+CC100) showed similar growth behavior and 3C-seq maps as the resized variants.
source: A control chimeric protein with wild-type arm length (Smc-CC334 Spn hinge+CC100) showed similar growth behavior and 3C-seq maps as the resized variants (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by spotting assays and 3C-seq data.

claim: Smc-CC253 showed only residual levels of inter-arm contacts extending only a few hundred kb from the replication origin.
source: With a shortened Smc protein, Smc-CC253, only residual levels of inter-arm contacts were noticeable, extending only few hundred kb from the replication origin (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq contact maps.

claim: A control chimeric protein with wild-type arm length and only the hinge domain replaced (Smc-CC334 Spn hinge) was only moderately affected for chromosome organization.
source: Another control chimeric protein with wild-type arm length and only the hinge domain replaced by the corresponding Streptococcus pneumoniae sequences (SmC-CC334 Spn hinge) was only moderately affected for chromosome organization (Figure 1D), implying that Smc arm modifications accounted for large parts of the defects in chromosome organization.
evidence: This is demonstrated by 3C-seq contact maps.

claim: Smc arm modifications account for large parts of the defects in chromosome organization.
source: Another control chimeric protein with wild-type arm length and only the hinge domain replaced by the corresponding Streptococcus pneumoniae sequences (SmC-CC334 Spn hinge) was only moderately affected for chromosome organization (Figure 1D), implying that Smc arm modifications accounted for large parts of the defects in chromosome organization.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing effects of hinge replacement versus arm modification.

claim: Engineered Smc variants are unable to properly co-align the two chromosome arms despite supporting growth and presumably chromosome segregation apparently normally.
source: We conclude that in contrast to wild-type Smc engineered Smc variants are unable to properly co-align the two chromosome arms despite supporting growth, and presumably chromosome segregation, apparently normally.
evidence: This is concluded from growth assays and 3C-seq data.

claim: Wild-type Smc efficiently aligned chromosome arms from a single strong parS site.
source: As expected from published work (Marbouty et al., 2015; Umbarger et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2015), wild-type Smc efficiently aligned chromosome arms from a single strong parS site (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by 3C-seq and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: All four Smc proteins with an extended Smc arm displayed clearly increased levels of inter-arm contacts when seven parS sites were inactivated.
source: Remarkably, all four Smc proteins with an extended Smc arm displayed clearly increased levels of inter-arm contacts (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq contact maps comparing strains with all parS versus single parS.

claim: Near the replication origin, chromosome arm alignment by modified Smc constructs was comparable to wild type.
source: Near the replication origin, chromosome arm alignment was comparable to wild type, while the inter-arm contacts were less frequent (or absent) further away from the replication origin with all modified Smc constructs (Figure 1C; for quantification, see Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq contact maps and quantified.

claim: Inter-arm contacts were less frequent or absent further away from the replication origin with all modified Smc constructs.
source: Near the replication origin, chromosome arm alignment was comparable to wild type, while the inter-arm contacts were less frequent (or absent) further away from the replication origin with all modified Smc constructs (Figure 1C; for quantification, see Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq contact maps and quantified.

claim: The shortened Smc variant (CC253) displayed more inter-arm contacts when seven parS sites were mutated.
source: The shortened Smc variant (CC253) also displayed more inter-arm contacts when the seven parS sites were mutated (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq contact maps.

claim: The removal of seven parS sites improved chromosome arm alignment by modified Smc proteins.
source: Thus, the removal of seven parS sites improved—rather than hindered—chromosome arm alignment by modified Smc proteins.
evidence: This is concluded from comparing 3C-seq maps with all versus single parS sites.

claim: The arc of contacts detected on the left arm of the chromosome was lost in all strains harboring only the –9kbparS site.
source: The arc of contacts detected on the left arm of the chromosome was lost in all strains harboring only the –9kbparS site (Figure 1C; Marbouty et al., 2015).
evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq contact maps and consistent with cited literature.

claim: The arc of contacts was lost when only –304kbparS site was mutated but not when its sequence was substituted for the –9kbparS sequence.
source: It was also lost when only –304kbparS site (parS-334) was mutated but not when its sequence was substituted for the –9kbparS sequence (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq contact maps.

claim: The –304kbparS site is unique in being relatively strong as well as distantly located from other strong parS sites.
source: Of note, the –304kbparS site is unique, in being relatively strong as well as distantly located from other strong parS sites (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is observed from the parS distribution map and ChIP data.

claim: DNA loop extrusion starting from the –304kbparS site is asymmetric, presumably due to a high likelihood of clashes with other Smc complexes and RNA polymerase.
source: DNA loop extrusion starting from this site is asymmetric, presumably due to a high likelihood of clashes with other Smc complexes and RNA polymerase (see scheme in Figure 1E and see below).
evidence: This is inferred from the arc pattern in 3C-seq maps and rifampicin experiments.

claim: The sequence of the –9kbparS site outperformed four other natural parS sequences and behaved equally well as an engineered consensus sequence at the ectopic location as judged by ChIP-qPCR.
source: The sequence of the –9kbparS site outperformed four other natural parS sequences and behaved equally well as an engineered consensus sequence at the ectopic location as judged by ChIP-qPCR (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-qPCR experiments.

claim: When two parSopt sites (–9kbparSopt and –304kbparSopt) were combined on the same chromosome, chromosome arm alignment by Smc-CC425 became inefficient.
source: When two parSopt sites (–9kbparSopt and –304kbparSopt) were combined on the same chromosome, chromosome arm alignment by Smc-CC425 became inefficient, producing a contact map similar to the one obtained with all parS sites present (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq contact maps.

claim: The arc originating from –304kbparS in strains carrying Smc-CC425 was less pronounced in the presence of rifampicin, indicating a partial relief of constraints on Smc translocation.
source: The arc originating from –304kbparS in strains carrying Smc-CC425 was less pronounced in the presence of rif, indicating a partial relief of constraints on Smc translocation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq contact maps with rifampicin treatment.

claim: Transcription contributes to the defects observed with Smc-CC425 in the presence of multiple parS sites.
source: This indicates that transcription contributes to the defects observed with Smc-CC425 in the presence of multiple parS sites.
evidence: This is inferred from the partial relief of defects upon rifampicin treatment.

claim: The presence of two or more parS sites hampers chromosome organization by Smc-CC425, conceivably because Smc-CC425 protein is more prone to collisions than wild-type Smc or less efficient in resolving them.
source: Altogether, we conclude that the presence of two or more parS sites hampers chromosome organization by Smc-CC425, conceivably because Smc-CC425 protein is more prone to collisions than wild-type Smc or less efficient in resolving them.
evidence: This is concluded from the pattern of defects with different parS configurations.

claim: Wild-type Smc-ScpAB displays highest enrichment on the chromosome in the replication origin region with long and shallow gradients of enrichment along both chromosome arms.
source: Wild-type Smc-ScpAB displays highest enrichment on the chromosome in the replication origin region with long and shallow gradients of enrichment along both chromosome arms (Gruber and Errington, 2009; Minnen et al., 2016), presumably generated by loading at parS, by translocation towards the replication terminus (ter) with some Smc being spontaneously unloaded from chromosome arms and the remaining fraction of Smc being unloaded by XerD near ter (Karaboja et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on cited ChIP studies and is consistent with current data.

claim: The chromosomal distribution pattern of Smc-ScpAB is presumably generated by loading at parS, translocation towards ter with some spontaneous unloading from chromosome arms, and the remaining fraction being unloaded by XerD near ter.
source: Wild-type Smc-ScpAB displays highest enrichment on the chromosome in the replication origin region with long and shallow gradients of enrichment along both chromosome arms (Gruber and Errington, 2009; Minnen et al., 2016), presumably generated by loading at parS, by translocation towards the replication terminus (ter) with some Smc being spontaneously unloaded from chromosome arms and the remaining fraction of Smc being unloaded by XerD near ter (Karaboja et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on cited studies and current understanding.

claim: Removal of seven parS sites had only a minor impact on the distribution of wild-type Smc-ScpAB as judged by ChIP-seq.
source: Removal of seven parS sites had only a minor impact on the distribution of wild-type Smc-ScpAB as judged by chromatin immunoprecipitation coupled to deep sequencing (ChIP-seq) using α-ScpB serum (Figure 2A, B, left panels).
evidence: This is observed in ChIP-seq profiles.

claim: The chromosomal distribution of Smc-CC425 showed hyper-enrichment near the replication origin and poor distribution towards the chromosome arms.
source: The chromosomal distribution of Smc-CC425 was markedly different (Figure 2A). It showed hyper-enrichment near the replication origin and poor distribution towards the chromosome arms.
evidence: This is observed in ChIP-seq profiles.

claim: The removal of seven parS sites substantially reduced the hyper-enrichment of Smc-CC425 near the origin and increased the signal on the chromosome arms.
source: Remarkably, the removal of seven parS sites substantially reduced the hyper-enrichment near the origin and increased the otherwise relatively low signal on the chromosome arms (Figure 2A, B, right panels, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is observed in ChIP-seq profiles.

claim: The hyper-enrichment of Smc in the replication origin region correlated with poor chromosome arm alignment.
source: The hyper-enrichment of Smc in the replication origin region thus correlated with poor chromosome arm alignment (Figure 1C).
evidence: This correlation is observed by comparing ChIP-seq and 3C-seq data.

claim: In the presence of multiple parS sites, the modified Smc coiled coil either impedes Smc translocation provoking frequent collisions and unproductive loop formation or increases the rate of unloading and subsequent reloading events in the origin region.
source: These results suggest that in the presence of multiple parS sites the modified Smc coiled coil either impedes Smc translocation provoking frequent collisions and unproductive loop formation or increases the rate of unloading and subsequent reloading events in the origin region.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the ChIP-seq and 3C-seq data.

claim: Both impediment of Smc translocation and increased unloading/reloading could explain the hyper-enrichment of Smc-CC425 in the origin region.
source: Both hypotheses could equally well explain the hyper-enrichment of Smc-CC425 in that region.
evidence: This is a logical inference about possible mechanisms.

claim: Smc and Smc-CC425 complexes were both enriched in an ~700 kb region centered on the replication origin after 20 min of ParB induction.
source: Smc and Smc-CC425 complexes were both found enriched in an ~700 kb region centered on the replication origin after 20 min of ParB induction by ChIP-seq analysis using α-ScpB serum (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is observed in ChIP-seq time-course experiments.

claim: For wild-type Smc, the enriched region increased in size over time, inferring a constant DNA translocation rate of roughly 500 bp/s at 30°C.
source: For wild-type Smc, the enriched region increased in size over time, inferring a constant DNA translocation rate of roughly 500 bp/s at 30°C.
evidence: This is calculated from ChIP-seq time-course data.

claim: The high enrichment of wild-type Smc near parS disappeared at later time points as Smc-ScpAB became more broadly distributed on the chromosome.
source: Notably, the high enrichment near parS disappeared at the later time points as Smc-ScpAB became more broadly distributed on the chromosome.
evidence: This is observed in ChIP-seq time-course experiments.

claim: The region of Smc-CC425 enrichment broadened during later time intervals, albeit with an apparently reducing rate.
source: The region of Smc-ScpAB enrichment also broadened in Smc-CC425 during the later time intervals, albeit with an apparently reducing rate.
evidence: This is observed in ChIP-seq time-course experiments.

claim: The origin region remained highly enriched in ScpB at later time points in Smc-CC425.
source: In addition, the origin region remained highly enriched in ScpB also at the later time points.
evidence: This is observed in ChIP-seq time-course experiments.

claim: Smc-CC425 was able to align chromosome arms in the ParB depletion/repletion experimental system, yet the alignment did not extend all the way to the ter region.
source: Using 3C-seq, we observed that Smc-CC425 was able to align chromosome arms in this experimental system, yet the alignment did not extend all the way to the ter region (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq time-course experiments.

claim: The onset of chromosome alignment and the rate of progress appeared somewhat reduced for Smc-CC425 when compared to wild-type Smc.
source: Moreover, the onset of chromosome alignment as well as the rate of progress appeared somewhat reduced when compared to wild-type Smc.
evidence: This is observed by comparing 3C-seq time-course data.

claim: The translocation rates of Smc-CC425 appeared to reduce at later time points, possibly due to increased spontaneous unloading.
source: Moreover, the translocation rates appeared to reduce at later timer points, possibly due to increased spontaneous unloading of Smc-CC425.
evidence: This is inferred from ChIP-seq and 3C-seq time-course data.

claim: Smc-CC425 efficiently accumulated in the replication origin region, but translocation to distal loci on the chromosome arms was hampered.
source: Regardless, these experiments demonstrate that Smc-CC425 efficiently accumulated in the replication origin region, but the translocation to distal loci on the chromosome arms was hampered.
evidence: This is concluded from ChIP-seq and 3C-seq time-course experiments.

claim: A simple explanation for the hyper-accumulation of Smc-CC425 in the replication origin region is an increase in spontaneous unloading of translocating Smc.
source: A simple explanation for the hyper-accumulation of Smc-CC425 in the replication origin region (in the presence of a single parS site) is an increase in spontaneous unloading of translocating Smc.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanistic explanation.

claim: Shorter periods of time spent translocating along chromosome arms increases the cytoplasmic pool of Smc and consequently the flux of loading.
source: With shorter periods of time spent translocating along the chromosome arms, the cytoplasmic pool of Smc increases and as a consequence so does the flux of loading, which—possibly together with a reduced translocation rate—leads to artificially increased enrichment near the parS site(s).
evidence: This is a logical inference about the relationship between residency time and loading flux.

claim: Increased loading flux leads to artificially increased enrichment near parS sites.
source: With shorter periods of time spent translocating along the chromosome arms, the cytoplasmic pool of Smc increases and as a consequence so does the flux of loading, which—possibly together with a reduced translocation rate—leads to artificially increased enrichment near the parS site(s).
evidence: This is a logical inference about the consequences of increased loading.

claim: Smc collisions would further exacerbate the Smc hyper-enrichment by hindering Smc translocation away from parS sites.
source: Such collisions would further exacerbate the Smc hyper-enrichment by hindering Smc translocation away from parS sites (Figure 2A, right panel).
evidence: This is a logical inference about the consequences of collisions.

claim: A reduced chromosome residency time and a reduced translocation rate may explain all phenotypic consequences of the Smc arm-modifications.
source: A reduced chromosome residency time and a reduced translocation rate may thus explain all phenotypic consequences of the Smc arm-modifications.
evidence: This is a proposed unified explanation for the observed phenotypes.

claim: Wild-type Smc displayed relatively low enrichment in the replication origin region even when all natural parS sites were present.
source: Wild-type Smc displayed relatively low enrichment in the replication origin region even when all natural parS sites were present (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is observed in ChIP-seq profiles.

claim: Control strains with a unique parSopt sequence at positions −9 kb, −304 kb, or +328 kb demonstrated extensive alignment of the respective flanking regions.
source: As expected, control strains with a unique parSopt sequence at positions −9 kb, at −304 kb, or at +328 kb (at amyE) demonstrated extensive alignment of the respective flanking regions (Figure 3A; Wang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq contact maps and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: The +328kbparSopt site, and to a lesser extent the –304kbparSopt site, resulted in asymmetric alignment of the flanking DNA probably due to the presence of clusters of highly transcribed genes in head-on orientation.
source: The +328kbparSopt site, and to a lesser extent the –304kbparSopt site, resulted in asymmetric alignment of the flanking DNA probably due to the presence of clusters of highly transcribed genes (including rDNA operons) in head-on orientation (Brandão et al., 2019).
evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq maps and explained by cited work on transcription effects.

claim: The frequency of contacts reaching beyond the replication origin is notably reduced with –304kbparSopt or +328kbparSopt, implying that the origin region acts as a semi-permissive barrier for Smc translocation.
source: Of note, the frequency of contacts reaching beyond the replication origin is notably reduced with –304kbparSopt or +328kbparSopt, implying that the origin region acts as a semi-permissive barrier for Smc translocation (or a Smc unloading site), as previously noted (Minnen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq maps and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: When two parS sites were combined on the chromosome, striking novel patterns of chromosome organization by wild-type Smc arose.
source: More importantly, when two parS sites were combined on the chromosome, striking novel patterns of chromosome organization by wild-type Smc arose (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq contact maps.

claim: Parallel secondary diagonals emerging from the two parS sites were detected when two parS sites were combined.
source: In all cases, parallel secondary diagonals emerging from the two parS sites were detected.
evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq contact maps.

claim: The pattern observed with –304kbparSopt and –9kbparSopt can largely be explained as a combination of contacts observed in strains with the corresponding single parS sites, with clearly reduced probability for contacts extending beyond the region demarcated by the parS sites.
source: The pattern observed with –304kbparSopt and –9kbparSopt can—to a large degree—be explained as a combination of contacts observed in strains with the corresponding single parS sites, however, with clearly reduced probability for contacts extending beyond the region demarcated by the parS sites.
evidence: This is observed by comparing 3C-seq contact maps.

claim: A small but noticeable fraction of Smc complexes managed to translocate towards and beyond the other parS site mostly unhindered.
source: A small but noticeable fraction of Smc complexes however apparently managed to translocate towards and beyond the other parS site mostly unhindered (as indicated by the largely unaltered position of the secondary diagonals).
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of secondary diagonals in 3C-seq maps.

claim: Treatment with rifampicin did not significantly alter the contact pattern with two parS sites apart from generating noisier maps.
source: Treatment with rif did not significantly alter the contact pattern (apart from generating noisier maps) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq experiments with rifampicin treatment.

claim: The contact maps involving the –304kbparSopt and +328kbparSopt sites showed additional contacts likely representing paired loops originating from collided Smc complexes loaded at opposite parS sites.
source: The contact maps involving the –304kbparSopt and +328kbparSopt sites showed additional contacts likely representing paired loops originating from collided Smc complexes loaded at opposite parS sites (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq contact maps and interpreted based on the experimental design.

claim: Wild-type Smc-ScpAB complexes rarely block one another when loaded from all natural parS sites with the notable exception of –304kbparS.
source: We conclude that wild-type Smc-ScpAB complexes rarely block one another when loaded from all natural parS sites (with the notable exception of –304kbparS).
evidence: This is concluded from the relatively normal 3C-seq patterns with all natural parS sites.

claim: When the distance between two strong parS sites was artificially increased, impacts arising from collisions and blockage became noticeable.
source: When the distance between two strong parS sites was artificially increased, however, impacts arising from collisions and blockage became noticeable.
evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq maps with repositioned parS sites.

claim: The blockage of Smc translocation was apparent from ChIP-seq analysis showing hyper-enrichment of Smc between two parS sites when compared to the single parS control.
source: The blockage of Smc translocation was also apparent from ChIP-seq analysis, which demonstrated hyper-enrichment of Smc between two parS sites (–304kbparSopt and –9kbparSopt or –9kbparSopt and +328kbparSopt) when compared to the single parS control (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is observed in ChIP-seq profiles.

claim: The effects of collisions on chromosome organization and Smc distribution are subdued with wild-type Smc but readily detectable upon repositioning of parS sites.
source: The effects of collisions on chromosome organization and Smc distribution are thus subdued with wild-type Smc but readily detectable upon repositioning of parS sites.
evidence: This is concluded from comparing different parS configurations.

claim: If Smc-CC425 fails to juxtapose chromosome arms due to an increased flux in the replication origin region, collisions may be rare in wild-type cells because of a high chromosome residency time and a limited pool of soluble Smc complexes, resulting in a low flux of Smc onto the chromosome.
source: If Smc-CC425 indeed fails to juxtapose chromosome arms due to an increased flux in the replication origin region, collisions may be rare in wild-type cells because of a high chromosome residency time and a limited pool of soluble Smc complexes, resulting in a low flux of Smc onto the chromosome.
evidence: This is a logical inference connecting the observations with Smc-CC425 to wild-type behavior.

claim: Artificially increasing the flux of Smc should lead to defects in chromosome organization with multiple parS sites but not with a single parS site if collisions are rare due to low flux.
source: If so, artificially increasing the flux of Smc should lead to defects in chromosome organization with multiple parS sites but not with a single parS site (as observed for Smc-CC425 under normal expression levels) (assuming that most Smc is loaded at parS).
evidence: This is a testable prediction based on the collision avoidance hypothesis.

claim: If Smc complexes efficiently traverse, reverse, or unload one another, then increased Smc levels would not result in defective translocation and chromosome organization.
source: If Smc complexes, however, were to efficiently traverse, reverse, or unload one another, then increased Smc levels would not result in defective translocation and chromosome organization.
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis that can be tested.

claim: Immunoblotting suggested a four- to fivefold increase in Smc and ScpB protein levels in the SMChigh strain when compared to wild type.
source: Immunoblotting suggested a four- to fivefold increase in Smc and ScpB protein levels in the SMChigh strain when compared to wild type (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting experiments.

claim: Chromosome arm co-alignment was strongly hampered by the presence of extra Smc complexes in the cell.
source: Chromosome arm co-alignment was strongly hampered—rather than improved—by the presence of extra Smc complexes in the cell (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq contact maps of SMChigh strains.

claim: A prominent arc was formed at the position of the –304kbparS site in the SMChigh strain.
source: A prominent arc was formed at the position of the –304kbparS site, and the secondary diagonal originating in the origin region was weak and diffuse in the SMChigh strain.
evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq contact maps.

claim: The defect in chromosome organization in SMChigh was fully restored by removal of seven parS sites.
source: This defect was fully restored, however, by removal of seven parS sites (with the remaining strong site being either –9kbparSopt or –304kbparSopt) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq contact maps.

claim: An additional minor secondary diagonal present on the right arm of the chromosome in SMChigh likely originated from Smc loading at the weak +1058kbparS site.
source: Note that an additional feature (a minor secondary diagonal) present on the right arm of the chromosome likely originated from Smc loading at the weak +1058kbparS site.
evidence: This is inferred from the position of the feature and knowledge of parS sites.

claim: The presence of two strong parS sites led to a new pattern of chromosome folding in the SMChigh strain with highly asymmetric alignment of DNA flanking the parS sites.
source: The presence of two strong parS sites (–9kbparSopt and –304kbparSopt) led to a new pattern of chromosome folding in the SMChigh strain. The alignment of DNA flanking the parS sites became highly asymmetric, presumably because Smc complexes loaded at opposite parS sites hinder each other (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq contact maps.

claim: Contacts corresponding to paired loops became clearly visible in SMChigh with two parS sites.
source: Moreover, the contacts corresponding to paired loops became clearly visible (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq contact maps.

claim: Contacts outside the parS-demarcated region were rare and spread out in SMChigh with two parS sites, and their center was shifted away from the parS sites.
source: Finally, contacts outside the parS-demarcated region were rare and spread out, and their center was shifted away from the parS sites.
evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq contact maps.

claim: Only a few Smc complexes loaded at one parS site managed to move beyond the other parS site in SMChigh.
source: The former indicated that only a few Smc complexes loaded at one parS site managed to move beyond the other parS site.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of contacts in 3C-seq maps.

claim: Smc complexes that moved from one parS site to the other experienced a strongly reduced translocation rate, presumably due to encounters with Smc complexes translocating in opposite orientation.
source: And if they did, they experienced a strongly reduced translocation rate when moving from parS site to the other, presumably due to encounters with and temporary (or partial) blockage by Smc complexes translocating in opposite orientation.
evidence: This is inferred from the shifted center of contacts in 3C-seq maps.

claim: The hindrance observed with two or all parS sites in SMChigh was not relieved by treatment with rifampicin, being consistent with Smc-Smc encounters rather than Smc-RNA polymerase encounters being mainly responsible.
source: Importantly, the hindrance observed with two or all parS sites being present was not relieved by treatment with rif, being consistent with the notion that Smc-Smc encounters rather than Smc-RNA polymerase encounters are mainly responsible for the impediment of translocation in SMChigh (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq experiments with rifampicin treatment.

claim: The localization of ParB to parS sites is largely unaffected by increased levels of Smc.
source: The α-ParB ChIP-seq demonstrated that the localization of ParB to parS sites is, as expected, largely unaffected by the increased levels of Smc (Figure 4E; Minnen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is observed in ChIP-seq experiments.

claim: The chromosomal distribution of ScpB was largely unaffected in SMChigh cells harboring a single –9kbparSopt site.
source: The chromosomal distribution of ScpB was also largely unaffected in SMChigh cells harboring a single –9kbparSopt site (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is observed in ChIP-seq profiles.

claim: In the presence of two or multiple additional parS sites, the enrichment of ScpB between the parS sites increased strongly in SMChigh.
source: However, in the presence of two or multiple additional parS sites, the enrichment between the parS sites increased strongly (Figure 4E, F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is observed in ChIP-seq profiles.

claim: The changes in ScpB distribution upon parS site removal are remarkably similar in Smc-CC425 and SMChigh.
source: The changes in ScpB distribution upon parS site removal are remarkably similar in Smc-CC425 and SMChigh (compare Figures 2B and 4E), supporting the notion that both modifications lead to more frequent blockage after collisions probably by the same mechanism: an increased flux of Smc in the vicinity of parS sites.
evidence: This is concluded by comparing ChIP-seq data from different experiments.

claim: Both Smc-CC425 and SMChigh modifications lead to more frequent blockage after collisions probably by the same mechanism: an increased flux of Smc in the vicinity of parS sites.
source: The changes in ScpB distribution upon parS site removal are remarkably similar in Smc-CC425 and SMChigh (compare Figures 2B and 4E), supporting the notion that both modifications lead to more frequent blockage after collisions probably by the same mechanism: an increased flux of Smc in the vicinity of parS sites.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the similar phenotypes.

claim: The alignment of DNA starting from –9kbparSopt site was hampered when a second parS site (–304kbparSopt) was present in synchronized loading experiments.
source: We found that the alignment of DNA starting from –9kbparSopt site was indeed hampered when a second parS site, –304kbparSopt, was present (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E), even more so than with continuous ParB expression (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq experiments with synchronized ParB induction.

claim: Under physiological conditions, collisions between Smc-ScpAB complexes are kept at a tolerable level by a low cellular abundance of Smc-ScpAB (~30 Smc dimers per chromosome or less), a high DNA translocation rate, an extended time of residency on the chromosome arms, and the preferential usage of a cluster of parS sites.
source: Under physiological conditions, collisions between Smc-ScpAB complexes are kept at a tolerable level by a low cellular abundance of Smc-ScpAB ~30 Smc dimers per chromosome or less (Wilhelm et al., 2015), a high DNA translocation rate, an extended time of residency on the chromosome arms, and the preferential usage of a cluster of parS sites (spanning ~60 kb region of the genome: –68kbparS, –63kbparS, –49kbparS, –9kbparS).
evidence: This is concluded from all the experimental observations and cited literature.

claim: Multiple parameters are fine-tuned to avoid Smc encounters, possibly rendering the resolution of Smc collisions unnecessary.
source: Thus, multiple parameters are fine-tuned to avoid Smc encounters, possibly rendering the resolution of Smc collisions unnecessary.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the overall findings of the study.

claim: Occasional loading of Smc at one of the more distal parS sites would quite often lead to collisions, resulting in contact maps with an arc-shaped pattern.
source: Occasional loading of Smc at one of the more distal parS sites however would quite often lead to collisions, thus resulting in contact maps with an arc-shaped pattern, such as observed for –304kbparS (the strongest of the distal parS sites) (Figure 1C; Brandão et al., 2020).
evidence: This is observed in 3C-seq maps and consistent with cited modeling work.

claim: The obvious defects in chromosome organization observed with altered parS positioning, elevated Smc levels, or engineered Smc proteins do not substantially impact bacterial growth.
source: The obvious defects in chromosome organization observed with altered parS positioning, elevated Smc levels, or engineered Smc proteins, however, do not substantially impact bacterial growth, suggesting that chromosome segregation is efficiently supported even with Smc collisions (and without chromosome arm alignment being detectable by population-averaging 3C methodology).
evidence: This is observed from growth assays showing normal or near-normal growth.

claim: Chromosome segregation is efficiently supported even with Smc collisions and without detectable chromosome arm alignment by 3C methodology.
source: The obvious defects in chromosome organization observed with altered parS positioning, elevated Smc levels, or engineered Smc proteins, however, do not substantially impact bacterial growth, suggesting that chromosome segregation is efficiently supported even with Smc collisions (and without chromosome arm alignment being detectable by population-averaging 3C methodology).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of normal growth despite organizational defects.

claim: Colliding Smc complexes might efficiently promote DNA disentanglement locally but hamper the global chromosome folding process.
source: Colliding Smc complexes might thus efficiently promote DNA disentanglement locally (with the help of DNA topoisomerases) but hamper the global chromosome folding process, possibly leading to large cell-to-cell variations in chromosome organization with likely knock-on effects on other cellular processes including nucleoid occlusion and cell division.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional consequences of collisions.

claim: The presence of multiple types of SMC complexes acting on the same chromosome likely aggravates the issue of collisions.
source: The presence of multiple types of SMC complexes acting on the same chromosome likely aggravates the issue of collisions.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the collision problem.

claim: In Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Smc-ScpAB appears to limit the loop extrusion activity of MksBEF but not vice versa.
source: In Pseudomonas aeruginosa, the impact of collisions seems to be dealt with by a hierarchy amongst two endogenous SMC complexes and a coordination of SMC activity with chromosome replication (Lioy et al., 2020). Smc-ScpAB appears to limit the loop extrusion activity of MksBEF but not vice versa.
evidence: This is based on a cited study of P. aeruginosa.

claim: When the heterologous E. coli MukBEF complex was introduced in P. aeruginosa in place of MksBEF, it blocked the activity of P. aeruginosa Smc-ScpAB but not the other way around.
source: When the heterologous Escherichia coli MukBEF complex was introduced in place of MksBEF, it blocked the activity of P. aeruginosa Smc-ScpAB but not the other way around.
evidence: This is based on a cited study.

claim: The hierarchy between SMC complexes is possibly given by the relative abundance of these complexes and differing chromosome association dynamics (residency times).
source: The hierarchy is possibly given by the relative abundance of these complexes and differing chromosome association dynamics (residency times).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed hierarchy.

claim: The parsimonious explanation for the observations is that neither wild-type nor modified Smc proteins are able to traverse one another.
source: The parsimonious explanation for our observations—not requiring the involvement of dedicated and potentially hazardous molecular transactions—is that neither wild-type nor modified Smc proteins are able to traverse one another.
evidence: This is proposed as the simplest explanation for the data.

claim: A recent study suggested that Smc traversal is needed to accurately recapitulate the relative abundance of long-range contacts observed with natural and artificial arrangements of parS sites.
source: A recent study describing Smc action in B. subtilis by simulations, however, suggested that Smc traversal is needed to accurately recapitulate the relative abundance of long-range contacts observed with natural and artificial arrangements of parS sites (similar to Figure 3B; Brandão et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on a cited modeling study.

claim: Direct observation of Smc traversal and of interlocking DNA loops (Z loops) on the bacterial chromosome is lacking.
source: Furthermore, direct observation of Smc traversal and of interlocking DNA loops (Z loops) on the bacterial chromosome is lacking.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of experimental evidence.

claim: A basic understanding of the molecular transactions necessary for Smc traversal is elusive.
source: Also, a basic understanding of the necessary molecular transactions is elusive.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of mechanistic understanding.

claim: A putative defect in traversal might contribute to the hyper-accumulation of Smc-CC425 in the replication origin region and the defective chromosome organization with multiple parS sites.
source: Nevertheless, the idea of Smc traversal is an intriguing proposition with potentially wide implications warranting serious consideration. A putative defect in traversal might contribute to the hyper-accumulation of Smc-CC425 in the replication origin region and the defective chromosome organization with multiple parS sites.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation for the observations.

claim: The nature and integrity of the Smc hinge domain and the adjacent coiled coil might be critical for the putative bypassing step in Smc traversal.
source: Assuming the validity of Smc traversal, it is tempting to speculate—on the basis of the observations with Smc-CC425—that the nature and the integrity of the Smc hinge domain and the adjacent coiled coil are critical for the putative bypassing step.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the Smc-CC425 phenotype.

claim: How Smc traversal might occur without the risk of establishing unwanted trans DNA linkages is totally unclear.
source: How Smc traversal might occur without the risk of establishing unwanted ('trans') DNA linkages yet is totally unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about a major mechanistic challenge.

claim: The presence of multiple parS sites likely improves the robustness of the chromosome segregation process.
source: The presence of multiple parS sites likely improves the robustness of the chromosome segregation process (Böhm et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on a cited study.

claim: Most bacteria have clustered parS sites within a 5–40 kb region and are sensitive to deleting or dispositioning them outside a tolerance region.
source: Most bacteria have clustered parS sites (within 5–40 kb region) and are sensitive to deleting or dispositioning them outside a tolerance region (Böhm et al., 2020; Lagage et al., 2016; Minnen et al., 2011; Tran et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on cited studies of parS distribution and function.

claim: Severe consequences of manipulating parS distribution include a longer generation time, an increased number of anucleate cells, and elongated cells.
source: Severe consequences of manipulating parS distribution include a longer generation time (when mksBEF is missing) (Lagage et al., 2016), an increased number of anucleate cells (Böhm et al., 2020) and elongated cells (Tran et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on cited studies.

claim: In Caulobacter crescentus, Smc translocates only ~600 kb away from parS.
source: In Caulobacter crescentus, Smc translocates only ~600 kb away from parS (Tran et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on a cited study.

claim: The partial chromosome arm alignment in C. crescentus is reminiscent of the observation with modified Smc proteins in B. subtilis.
source: The partial chromosome arm alignment in C. crescentus is reminiscent of the observation with modified Smc proteins in B. subtilis.
evidence: This is a comparison drawn between different organisms.

claim: A shorter chromosome residency time or a lower translocation rate of Smc-ScpAB is acceptable when parS sites are tightly clustered or when combined with a single parS site.
source: It is tempting to speculate that a shorter chromosome residency time or a lower translocation rate of Smc-ScpAB is acceptable when parS sites are tightly clustered or when combined with a single parS site.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation connecting different observations.

claim: Some bacterial genomes harbor multiple parS sites that are quite widely scattered on the genome.
source: Nevertheless, some bacterial genomes harbor multiple parS sites that are quite widely scattered on the genome.
evidence: This is an observation about bacterial genome organization.

claim: The scattered parS distribution is restricted to few lineages on the phylogenetic tree of bacteria, including Bacilli.
source: Intriguingly, the scattered parS distribution is restricted to few lineages on the phylogenetic tree of bacteria, including Bacilli (Livny et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on a cited genomic survey.

claim: The scattering of parS sites likely serves a dedicated purpose in the lifestyles of bacteria with scattered parS sites, in B. subtilis possibly during sporulation.
source: The scattering of parS sites likely serves a dedicated purpose in the lifestyles of these bacteria, in B. subtilis possibly during sporulation when large chunks of the genome (~1 Mb, i.e., about a quarter of the genome) are captured at the cell pole to promote entrapment of the chromosome in the pre-spore (Wu and Errington, 1998).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on cited work on sporulation.

claim: Chromosome capture during sporulation might benefit from the condensation of the replication origin involving Smc collisions rather than an alignment of chromosome arms.
source: This process might benefit from the condensation of the replication origin (possibly involving Smc collisions as observed here) rather than an alignment of chromosome arms.
evidence: This is a speculative functional interpretation.

claim: Chromosome arm alignment is lost when DNA replication is artificially blocked and replaced by smaller loops formed at individual parS sites.
source: Consistent with this notion, chromosome arm alignment is lost when DNA replication is artificially blocked (as naturally occurring during sporulation) and replaced by smaller loops formed at individual parS sites (Marbouty et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on cited studies.

claim: A simple explanation for the altered pattern of chromosome folding during replication blockage is an increased rate of Smc collisions due to an elevated protein-to-DNA ratio.
source: A simple explanation for this altered pattern of chromosome folding during replication blockage (and possibly also during sporulation) would be an increased rate of Smc collisions due to an elevated (Smc) protein-to-DNA ratio.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanistic explanation.

claim: The process of Smc DNA translocation is finely tuned to keep the probability of Smc encounters at a low level, presumably to enable extensive DNA loop extrusion without the need to resolve Smc collisions.
source: Altogether, our results strongly suggest that the process of Smc DNA translocation is finely tuned to keep the probability of Smc encounters at a low level, presumably to enable extensive DNA loop extrusion without the need to resolve Smc collisions.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the experimental observations.
